extracted.intended_audience: authors of humorous writing and satirical essayists (readers/periodical-writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for composing humour and satire in periodical essays: how to distinguish true from false humour, choose targets and tone, and use moral purpose and judgement in comic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of true humour
rubrics_metrics.description: True humour is the offspring of Truth and Good Sense (a mixture of Wit and Mirth); it exhibits regularity of thought, is under the check of reason, and often appears serious while making others laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour should be guided by the nicest judgment: not a raving incoherence or delirious mirth. True humour mixes wit and mirth (Wit = good sense; Mirth = jocularity). It often looks grave while provoking laughter; it requires an orderly structure of thought and moral grounding. Avoid the belief that mere extravagant conceits or absurd inconsistent ideas constitute humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of false humour
rubrics_metrics.description: False humour (a counterfeit of true humour) stems from falsehood and nonsense; it displays buffoonery, mimicry, indiscriminate ridicule, lack of reason, and personal attacks rather than targeting vice or folly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay lists five chief signs of false humour: (1) excessive apish tricks and buffooneries; (2) over-reliance on mimicry that exposes anyone (virtue or vice) for spectacle; (3) unlucky tendency to ridicule friends and foes alike (biting the hand that feeds it); (4) absence of rational purpose — ludicrous for its own sake; (5) ridicule aimed at persons rather than at vices or faults in themselves. False humour is loud, excessive in laughter, and typically spurious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour must be under the check of reason and regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour requires an underlying order and rational control — a 'certain Regularity of Thought' — and must not be mere caprice or incoherent extravagance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should subject comic invention to judgment: freedom in humour increases the need for careful direction. Delirious or incoherent mirth signals a disordered mind rather than humour. Read over one's work: if it is nonsense to oneself, it will fail as humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical target principle — attack vice, not private persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire should aim at vice and folly in general (multitudes, customs, fashions) rather than exposing particular private intrigues or aiming to hurt individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer promises not to draw faulty characters that do not fit at least a thousand people, and to write in the spirit of benevolence. Reprehend vices that are too trivial for law and too fantastical for the pulpit, but avoid naming or publishing particulars that target single persons' reputations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate targets of satire (consider rank and public good)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should consider which classes or spheres are appropriate objects of raillery: vanity and luxury of courts and the follies of the stage are proper subjects; high and conspicuous stations are especially fit for reproof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different commentators in the Club advise different provinces for satire (City vs Court). The conservative view: attack what is most public and influential — vices in high stations — because chastising these serves the public. However, be mindful of social context and prudence (e.g., some advise avoiding the Army or certain respected country classes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid satirizing the poor or those already depressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Targeting those in low condition or poverty with ridicule aggravates their pains and does not serve the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cleric's counsel: do not chiefly expose the depressed or poor; satire aimed at the already oppressed only increases suffering and lacks usefulness. Prefer to reprehend follies that are social or fashionable rather than to mock misfortune or poverty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of public satire: attack multitudes and systemic faults
rubrics_metrics.description: When exercising satire, prefer general exemplars and collective follies rather than individual lampoons; treat libellers and lampooners as legitimate targets when they abuse others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states he will 'attack Multitudes' and that it is natural to retaliate against libellers and lampooners, treating them publicly. The method is to scandalize practices and fashions in aggregate, not to publish private intrigues — thereby balancing correction and benevolence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical representation guideline: show human affectation not grotesque monsters
rubrics_metrics.description: The theatre should endeavour to show 'humane Life' and represent people made monstrous by affectation and industry, rather than admit gross fantastical monsters or unnatural appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A petition from the playhouse expresses a desire to remove 'monsters' and exhibit only men transformed into monsters by their own affectation; stage effects and grotesques that do not contribute to representation of manners should be cashiered. Use theatrical spectacle to expose fashionable distortions (mien and gesture) rather than gratuitous oddities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading selection for women: prefer books that enlighten and rectify the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: A lady's reading should include works that enlighten the understanding and rectify the passions, not merely romances that divert the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leonora's example: although she reads widely among romances and has formed her house and taste accordingly, true improvement comes from books that educate the mind and moral feelings. The author intends to recommend particular books proper for the improvement of the sex, implying criteria for selection (moral and intellectual edification over mere diversion).
